prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, enabling frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I still place B049 first. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal removed the central trade-off of neutral-atom clocks: thousands of atoms can be interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free with the lattice light shift cancelled, so statistical averaging and systematic control improve together. The performance is a measured quantity, not a promise: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 confirmed in several independent laboratories and in remote clock comparisons. Experimentally this is the strongest case on the shortlist, because the evidence is a number that other groups reproduce. It has already opened new measurements: height differences resolved at the centimetre level (relativistic geodesy), tests of the constancy of fundamental constants, searches for ultralight dark matter, and the basis for redefining the SI second. Four of six members who ranked it placed it in their top three, which is a broader base than any other candidate has. Two named laureates make a clean configuration with an identifiable pair of contributions, the founding idea (Katori) and the drive to the performance frontier and many-body clocks (Ye).
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is overlap and the credit history. Frequency combs (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and ion control (Wineland, 2012) already honoured the precision-timekeeping lineage, and Ye's contributions to combs and cold-atom spectroscopy are intertwined with the clock work, so a committee could see this as an extension of a recognized line rather than a new discovery. Also, Ye's group is the record holder but other contributors (for example Takamoto and Hong in Katori's group, the SYRTE, PTB, NIST and Boulder strontium and ytterbium clock efforts, and Lemonde's early work) did essential realization steps, and the name assignment is contestable. Finally, a measurement tool is easier to honour once its major scientific harvest (redefinition of the second, geodesy at scale, constants tests) has been delivered, and some of that is still prospective.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B049 fifth and worries that precision measurement already received prizes in 2005 and 2012, so priority for the clock is lower, and he leads with circuit QED and trapped ions.
responses.response: I accept that the overlap concern is real, but I think it argues about framing, not about eligibility. The 2005 prize recognized the comb as the ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize recognized control of single quantum systems; neither covers the neutral-atom many-particle lattice clock, which is a distinct physical idea (magic wavelength) with a distinct measurement outcome (1e-18 stability reached through averaging over many atoms). I also note your own worry about circuit QED, that the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize makes B038 too close in time, is a stronger overlap argument than anything against B049, since that is the same platform and the same decade. My reservation about B038 is the reverse: credit among four names is unresolved and the discovery is arguably a derivative of cavity QED for which a prize was given in 2012.

responses.point: Pearce puts Halzen and IceCube first as a new observational window and ranks B049 third, while saying atomic precision measurement is outside his expertise and he defers to colleagues.
responses.response: I agree that IceCube is a genuine new window, and I would not dismiss it; the diffuse flux detection is a robust, well-characterized measurement. My two reservations are about the configuration and the maturity of the story. First, a one-name prize for a collaboration of several hundred people forces the committee to say that one person's leadership defines the discovery, and the project's own early history (AMANDA, the role of other founders and spokespersons) complicates that. Second, the source identification is still partial and has only one instrument, so the physics outcome behind the discovery is less settled than the lattice clock numbers. I would keep B047 as a serious candidate, but I think B049 has the cleaner attribution and the more reproducible evidence, and I would be glad to hear whether you think the single-name issue is resolvable.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B049 first as a conceptual step beyond single-ion clocks and flags that the committee must decide whether to see it as honouring clocks together with the 2012 prize or as incremental.
responses.response: I agree with your ranking and with the framing of the question. My answer on the incremental point is that the lattice clock changes what is achievable, not just how well an existing method performs: single-ion clocks are limited by one particle's signal-to-noise, and the lattice clock beats that limit by a mechanism that did not exist before the magic-wavelength idea. Your caution about Ye's presence in the ultracold-molecule candidate is worth noting for the later rounds, though that candidate is not on this shortlist, so no double counting arises here. Where I would qualify your view is that the physics is also more settled than the sensing applications, so I would not lean on the redefinition of the second as the main argument.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B024 first as a clean discovery from nature, the last neutrino mixing angle being surprisingly large, with a stable interpretation and wide confirmation, and ranks B049 eighth.
responses.response: I find B024 a strong and well-measured result, and I agree that the large theta-13 was a surprise that shaped the next generation of experiments. My difficulty is the prize history: the 2015 prize was for neutrino oscillations and the committee may see this as a determination of a missing parameter in a framework already honoured. The credit among Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz is also delicate, and the three names exclude Double Chooz's leadership and the T2K appearance result. I have kept B024 as an alternative because the discovery quality is clear. I would ask you how you rank its novelty against the clock, since I regard the clock as having a broader effect on other fields of physics.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.

Whether a two-name prize for Katori and Ye is the fairest allocation given other groups (Takamoto, Hong, Lemonde, PTB, NIST) who contributed to the realization; I rely on recollection for exact roles and have not verified record uncertainties.
Whether the main scientific harvest (second redefinition, geodesy at scale, dark-matter and constants limits) is mature enough or still prospective.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B049. I did my PhD in Lund with a stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is a 2005 laureate in the frequency-comb lineage next to Ye's group at JILA, which is a distant mentoring connection rather than a recusal issue. I have a research connection to quantum memories in rare-earth crystals, which would be relevant for some quantum-information candidates (B001, B044), though not for the preferred configuration. I also note my WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where my colleague Johansson is based, relevant only to circuit-QED candidates (B038).
